report.headline: Projected to a marginal NBA role, with the shooting-efficiency forecast unreliable by the model's own admission

projection.text: Usage rate is projected at 11.9% in the NBA, down from 15.5% in the 2018-19 G League season and well below the 20.1% minutes-weighted NBA average that season.

risks.text: Projected NBA usage of 11.9% is below both the z-preservation baseline (14.7%, what the same relative standing would imply) and close to the naive 0.75x-scaling folk rule (11.6%), suggesting a shrunken, low-usage role is the model's central expectation rather than an artifact of one method.

The true shooting projection (56.4%) cannot be treated as informative: the model's out-of-fold error (4.7%) is identical to that of simply predicting the league mean, meaning it offers no edge over a trivial guess for this metric.

Source-season playmaking indicators were modest — 1.747 assists per 75 possessions and a 7.0% assist rate — with over two-thirds of shot attempts coming from three, pointing to a specialized, low-usage offensive profile even before accounting for the league jump.
The estimate rests on only 45 historical GL->NBA transitions and two full seasons elapsed between the source season and the move, both of which widen the uncertainty around any single projection.

strengths.text: Source-season true shooting was 61.0%, a full standard deviation above the G League average that year.

The player already sat well above their own league's average usage entering the move, consistent with the typical selection effect for players who make this transition (players who move average +0.27 sd above their league).

For usage rate specifically, the fitted GL->NBA slope of 0.529 indicates roughly half of a player's standing above the G League average tends to carry over to the NBA, and the model beats a trivial league-mean baseline on this metric (3.3% error vs. 4.3%).

uncertainty.text: The 80% prediction interval for usage runs from 6.4% to 17.4% — a span of roughly two standard deviations of NBA usage (5.5%) — so the model can say this player projects below average but cannot pin down where within a wide low-usage band; the true shooting projection of 56.4% should not be trusted at all, since the model's error there (4.7%) is no better than simply guessing the league mean.
